note: Optional learner-facing See-it mini-lessons for academy foundation sessions. 2–4 sentences in plain adult English. Not Sefaria-as-instruction. The renderer also accepts skill.teach / item.teach; if those are missing, academy-session-lesson.mjs falls back here, then to a built-in source-type lesson. The `genres` block below adds a plain-adult mini-lesson for each basic kind of Jewish text (Torah verse, Mishnah, Gemara, commentary), each with one short on-page excerpt (Hebrew + translation, not a Sefaria link), to feed the See-it mini-lesson's genre gallery for fnd-orient-source-type. Every non-L0 starter-set skill has a `teach` entry so academy-session See-it is never empty; Layer 0 decode uses glyph UI and is held out of this bank.

teach.fnd-orient-source-type: Jewish texts come in a few basic kinds, and you can often tell which one you are looking at from its shape — before you translate every word. A Torah verse usually tells or commands in the Bible’s own voice. A Mishnah states a compact rule; the Gemara then asks about that rule and argues it. Commentary talks about the text from the side; a prayer addresses God in praise or petition, rather than arguing a rule.
teach.fnd-orient-page-geography: On a printed Jewish study page, the source you are learning usually sits in a large central or top block, and later notes sit around it. The main block is the text itself; the surrounding columns are talk about the text. Find the block that would still make sense if everything around it were removed — that is the primary text. On a Talmud page, a small marker (גמ׳) often shows where the compact rule ends and the discussion of it begins.
teach.fnd-orient-speaker: A source is often a conversation, not one speaker. Look first for names and words like "said" or "says"; everything after that belongs to that voice until the next name appears. If no name is attached, you are hearing the book's own narrator, not a quoted person.
teach.fnd-orient-unit-boundary: Ideas in these sources come in units, not as one unbroken stream. A new unit usually starts when a new name appears, a new question is asked, a new case begins, or the topic clearly shifts. Mark that seam before you try to understand the whole page at once.
teach.fnd-orient-question-present: Not every line is telling you something. Some lines are asking — they expect an answer, a reason, or a source. A word like מֵאֵימָתַי ("from when") or אֵיפֹה ("where") is a tell; a line that simply states a practice or a rule is not asking. Before you translate, mark each line as a question or a statement.
teach.fnd-signal-known-words: A small set of words shows up again and again — אָמַר ("said"), בָּרוּךְ ("blessed"), מֵאֵימָתַי ("from when"), שְׁמַע ("hear"), עַד ("until"). If you can recognize those on sight, you stop decoding every letter and can watch what the sentence is doing. Look for that short list first in every new excerpt.
teach.fnd-signal-question-words: Certain short words flag a question and hint at the kind of answer that should follow. A word meaning "what" often wants a definition; a word meaning "why" wants a reason; a word meaning "from when" wants a time; a phrase meaning "from where do we know this" wants a cited source. Spot that signal first, then predict the shape of the reply. In a stretch of discussion — a sugya — those question-words map what the argument is hunting for.
teach.fnd-signal-name-formulas: Jewish sources often hand a line to a named voice with a short formula such as "Rabbi X says", "Rav said", "the Sages say", or "the words of Rabbi X". That formula does not argue; it assigns those words to that person. Mark every such formula so you know whose claim you are reading.
teach.fnd-signal-connectors: Tiny words steer the argument: words that mean "therefore," "but," "rather," "and then," "as it says," or "this teaches". They tell you whether the next clause adds, opposes, or cites. If you read only the connectors first, you can feel the shape of the argument before every word is clear.
teach.fnd-signal-quotation: Sometimes a source stops speaking in its own voice and brings in another text — a verse or an earlier teaching — as evidence. Citation formulas such as "as it is written" or "as it says" are the tell. Treat the words that follow as borrowed, not as the current speaker's own sentence.
teach.fnd-role-question-vs-answer: Notice three jobs a line can have. A line that asks — from when, who is wise, why — is a question. The next line that supplies the time, the definition, or the reason is its answer. A line that only repeats earlier wording so the discussion can probe it is a restatement, not a new answer.
teach.fnd-role-example: After a rule, a source often drops into a concrete case: "someone who", "an ox that", "a booth that is higher than", or a short scene such as two people holding one object, or a poor person standing outside and a householder inside. That case is not a new rule; it is a worked example testing the rule just stated. Point to the example and name the rule it is illustrating.
teach.fnd-role-quotation-bounds: A citation signal such as "as it is said", or a quoted word followed by a dash, marks the start of borrowed text. Read forward until the voice clearly returns to the current source: everything inside those edges is the cited text, and everything after is the speaker using it. If you miss the closing edge, you will treat the speaker's own words as if the cited source said them.
teach.fnd-role-ruling-vs-discussion: Notice whether the reader is left with one option or several. A line that tells you what to do and closes the alternatives — one should rise, one searches for leaven — is a ruling. A stretch that weighs two or more views and keeps them standing — these and those are the words of the living God, unfit followed by a sage who still deems it fit, or three named cutoff times that all still stand — is a discussion.
teach.fnd-case-actors: Before asking what a case means, list the people or parties as a cast and attach one action to each. Two people holding one garment are two claimants; a host, a guest, and a man invited by mistake are three actors in a feast; an ox that gores acts for its owner; Jonah fleeing a command is another named actor. The legal or moral question sits on that who-did-what list, not instead of it.
teach.fnd-case-what-happens: Tell the situation as a one-sentence story in ordinary words: who, did what, to whom. Two people holding a garment is already that sentence; a booth taller than twenty cubits is someone with a too-tall booth, not yet a verdict. Say what happens plainly before you argue about rights, meaning, or whether the booth counts.
teach.fnd-case-restate: Restating is more than summarizing: close the text and retell the case in your own words, then reopen and check what you dropped. A faithful restatement keeps who acted, what happened, and any split or condition — without copying the original phrasing or adding a verdict the text did not give. If a retelling changes the outcome or drops a party, it is not yet faithful.
teach.fnd-case-uncertainty: Notice the open question the case still needs in order to decide — not a conclusion. A from-when or until-when is a cutoff time not yet settled; two claimants with no proof leave ownership unknown; two people claiming the same child leave parentage unknown; a booth taller than twenty cubits leaves whether it still counts unsettled. Name that missing piece as an open question.
teach.fnd-arg-claim: A claim is the sentence the source wants you to accept or act on. Before judging the argument, finish "This source claims that" in one plain line. Notice what is not a claim: a timing question, a citation (as it is written), or an attribution (Rabbi X says).
teach.fnd-arg-evidence-role: When a source cites another text — as it is written, as it is said — that citation has a job. Notice whether the verse backs the claim (supports), pulls the other way (challenges), draws a distinction (clarifies), or splits the claim into cases. After the citation, the claim should feel stronger, weaker, narrower, or split — say which.
teach.fnd-arg-objection: An objection is a pushback: it threatens the claim, the reason for the claim, or how far the claim reaches. Notice a follow-up that says the reason fails in another case, or that the plan would also sweep away the innocent, or that a rescue plan has so far made things worse. Name exactly what would break if the first claim stood unchanged; answering comes next.
teach.fnd-arg-response: After an objection, notice how the source answers. It may deny the objection (it is not in heaven), limit it to a narrower case (a booth above twenty cubits is not the ordinary dwelling), or accept the point and adjust the original claim (the destruction plan is withdrawn, or the city is spared if enough innocent people are found). Compare the claim before and after, and name which of those three happened.
teach.fnd-arg-unresolved: Not every discussion ends with a winner. Notice endings that stop without deciding: a marker תֵּיקוּ meaning "let it stand", two voices still pressing, a line that says a disagreement is meant to last, or a reply that answers with a further question rather than a verdict. If no one got the last word, name the tension left standing — that openness is the point, not a missing page.
teach.fnd-context-genre-expectations: Jewish sources come in different genres, and each asks to be read differently. A psalm, blessing, or story (aggadah) offers image and meaning — a shepherd and still waters, Blessed are You — not a binding ruling. A legal code (halakhah) states what to do and rewards precise reading. A single passage can hold both, so match what you ask of each block.
teach.fnd-resp-learning-vs-ruling: Reading a source of Jewish law teaches you what the text says, not what you personally must do. Notice two questions: what have I learned on this page, and what should I do in my own life. A line that states a practice, or that lays out more than one view, is still learning until a competent teacher who knows your situation gives a ruling.

torah.name: Torah verse
torah.teach: The Torah is Scripture itself — the Five Books — in its own voice. A Torah verse tells a story or gives a command directly; it is the source that everything else discusses, not a discussion of the source. You will not find a rabbi's name attached to the verse or a back-and-forth argument inside it.

example.hebrew: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
example.translation: Hear, O Israel: the LORD is our God, the LORD is one.

mishnah.name: Mishnah
mishnah.teach: The Mishnah is the first great rabbinic law book, edited about eighteen centuries ago. It states practice in short, dense Hebrew, and often records where named sages disagree. It usually just states the rule; it does not quote proof-verses or argue at length — that comes afterward, in the Gemara.

example.translation: From when may one recite the Shema in the evening?

gemara.name: Gemara
gemara.teach: The Gemara is the long discussion that grew up around the Mishnah — together they make the Talmud. It is largely in Aramaic and moves by questions: it asks what the Mishnah means, raises objections, and brings proofs. Where the Mishnah states a rule, the Gemara probes it.

example.translation: Where does the Tanna stand [what is he discussing], that he teaches 'from when'?

commentary.name: Commentary
commentary.teach: A commentary explains another text from the side, rather than being that text. It quotes a word or phrase from the base source and then explains it — Rashi's notes on the Torah and Talmud are the classic example. On the page it sits around the main text, keyed to it line by line.

example.hebrew: בְּרֵאשִׁית — אֵין הַמִּקְרָא הַזֶּה אוֹמֵר אֶלָּא דָּרְשֵׁנִי
example.translation: 'In the beginning' — this verse says nothing other than 'interpret me.'
